full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass. The agents are a textbook Vicsek model. The field never acts back on them, so it is just a time-integrated picture of where the flock has been. Both measured features come from Vicsek clustering, which is well documented. I found nothing new in the behaviour.

**1. Breaking down the program**
- Rule 1 is the Vicsek alignment rule: each agent turns to the average heading of agents within a fixed radius, with angular noise and constant speed on a wrap-around square. That is the standard model. At each time step, a particle reorients itself along the average direction of propulsion of particles in a unit radius around it, with some external noise preventing perfect alignment.
- Rule 2 only adds a field that agents deposit into. It diffuses slowly, never decays, and nothing reads it, so it cannot change what the agents do.
- The sub-program results fit this:
  - **Rule 2 only:** agents wander independently, so deposits spread out evenly. The field has low variation (f_std 0.44) and about 4 small blobs.
  - **Rule 1 only:** there is no field, so the field numbers are essentially zero (f_std 0.013).
  - **Full program:** alignment packs the deposits into one dominant patch, giving high variation (f_std 4.25) and about 1 blob. Neither rule alone does this, as you would expect when the field is simply recording the flock.

**2. The behaviour is documented**
- Clustering and travelling dense groups in the ordered Vicsek phase are standard results. A coexistence region delimited by two binodal lines separates the disordered "gas" phase present at strong noise/low density from the ordered collectively moving "liquid"... In this region, particles form dense, ordered bands ("microphases") that travel in the remaining sparse gas. The transition is actually 1st order, with an intermediate coexistence regime of high density ordered bands traveling in a low density disordered background. This was established by Grégoire & Chaté, PRL 92, 025702 (2004).
- Your settings are low noise (0.3 rad) and low density (about 0.1 agents per unit area, or about 2.8 neighbours within radius 3). That fits the low-noise single-cluster regime: a single cluster that contains a macroscopic fraction of the particles in the system occurs in the hitherto unexplored regime of very low noise intensities. Further decrease of the noise allow clusters to merge in larger ones. This would explain why the field ends up with about one blob.
- Coupled agent–field models do exist, such as autochemotaxis and trail-following. There, the deposited chemical field diffuses and memory is lost on finite timescales. All of those, though, have the field feeding back on the agents. Yours has no feedback, so nothing new can happen in the field itself.

**3. Is there a twist?** The only one is geometric. A coherent flock moving straight on a wrap-around square keeps passing over the same track, and with no decay the field turns into a single bright streak or blob. That follows directly from "a flock, integrated over time, on a torus". I didn't find a paper that names it, but it is a consequence of the known behaviour, not new behaviour. The weaker effect at 3× run length fits slow diffusion blurring the streak and the flock's direction slowly drifting.

**4. Genuine or artifact?** The field itself is inert: it records positions and changes nothing. But the features are not noise or a numerical glitch. They are big and stable effects (more than 3 spreads from the knock-out, and they hold at 4× area and 3× run length). They faithfully reflect real emergent behaviour: Vicsek flocking and clustering. So the underlying pattern is genuine and emergent, but the field adds nothing beyond it. Also note that f_std partly grows just because deposits keep piling up with no decay.

**Searches I ran:** Vicsek bands and clustering in the ordered phase (Grégoire & Chaté), and Vicsek agents depositing into a diffusing field with one-way coupling.
